wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e111.summary: Poses a question annexed to the third principal question: whether the habit of theology is really one in number.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e118.summary: First argument for numerical unity, from Metaphysics X: the first in every genus is most one and simple. Theology is the first among intellectual habits, since habits are ordered by their subjects and God, theology's subject, is first among subjects. So theology is maximally one, and since some habit is numerically one, theology is too.
claims: The first in every genus is maximally one and simple (argument).
Habits are ordered according to the order of their subjects (argument).

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e140.summary: Second argument: one genus of subject has one science, and theology's subject, God, is numerically one, so its habit is numerically one.
claims: One genus of subject has one science (argument).

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e147.summary: Third argument: theology is as unified as any naturally acquired science, and some naturally acquired science is numerically one.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e164.summary: Argument to the contrary: distinct acts cause distinct habits, and there are distinct acts concerning distinct theological truths, so there are distinct habits.
claims: Distinct acts cause distinct habits.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e173.summary: Reports a view (Thomist in character) that theology is one because a science's unity follows the unity of its power and habit with respect to the formal, not material, object. Theology considers everything insofar as divinely revealed, and all revealed truths share this one formal ratio.
claims: The unity of a science follows the formal ratio of its object (reported).
All of theology's objects share the formal ratio of being divinely revealed (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e193.summary: Ockham argues the view errs in several ways. First, neither the unity of power or habit can be inferred from the unity of the formal object, nor their distinction from the distinction of formal objects.
claims: Unity of formal object does not entail unity of power or habit.
Distinction of formal objects does not entail distinction of power or habit.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e204.summary: First proof of the first point: the same thing under the same formal ratio is the object of sense and intellect, since nothing is sensible that the higher power cannot attain under the same ratio.
claims: The same thing under the same formal ratio is an object of both sense and intellect.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e215.summary: Further proofs. Unless sense and intellect share an object under the same ratio, there is no reason the intellect's act should presuppose sense's rather than the reverse. Also, there are no distinct rationes in reality (they would be distinct things). The same object under the same ratio belongs to intuitive and abstractive cognition, to intellect and will (nothing unknown can be willed), and to science, error and opinion (one person can err about a conclusion another knows). Conversely, sight has distinct formal objects, white and black, yet is one power, since each can be apprehended with nothing else apprehended.
claims: There are no really distinct rationes in things apart from distinct things.
Intuitive and abstractive cognition share the same object under the same ratio.
Intellect and will share their object, since nothing unknown is willed.
Science, opinion and error can concern the same conclusion.
One power can have distinct formal objects, as sight has white and black.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e261.summary: Objection: white and black are material objects of sight, color is the formal object, and nothing is seen except under the ratio of color.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e271.summary: Ockham asks what a 'material' object means. If it is the subject of the formal ratio (as man, ass and wood are subjects of color), white and black are not material objects, since they are colors, not subjects of color. So one power has distinct formal objects. If it means something contained under the formal ratio, there is no such thing for a habit of complex propositions, and the claim reduces to the uncontested point that distinct adequate objects imply distinct powers.
claims: White and black are colors, not subjects of color, and so are formal objects.
Distinct adequate objects imply distinct powers, but that is not the issue.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e304.summary: Further: 'nothing is seen except under the ratio of color' means either that nothing is seen unless colored, in which case white can still be seen with nothing else apprehended, or that the ratio of color itself, as distinct from lower rationes, is seen. That is impossible, because such a ratio is universal and exists in the intellect, so it cannot be apprehended by sense.
claims: A universal ratio exists only in the intellect and cannot be sensed.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e328.summary: Further: when white is seen under the ratio of color, that ratio is either particular or universal. If particular, it is just this whiteness, since there are no distinct particular rationes in it (which on the opponent's denial of formal distinction would be distinct things), so the whiteness is seen under its own ratio. If universal, sight would apprehend a universal.
claims: There are no distinct particular rationes within a single whiteness.
Sight cannot apprehend a universal.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e348.summary: Further: some habit concerns a complex proposition, yet each term under its own ratio is an object, so formal unity of object is not what makes a habit one.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e355.summary: Attacks the view's minor premise: being divinely revealable is not theology's formal object. Otherwise every geometrical conclusion, being revealable, would belong to theology. Also, on the opponent's own view God under the ratio of deity is the subject of theology.
claims: Being divinely revealable is not the formal ratio of theology's object.
Every geometrical conclusion is divinely revealable.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e368.summary: Reports a second opinion (Scotist in character) reaching the same conclusion: a science considering many attributes of one subject under one formal mode of consideration is one habit, as simple as any affective habit such as temperance or a whiteness. The first act generating it produces the habit's whole reality in the lowest degree. Cognitive habits differ from affective ones only in being generated and increased by acts of different species (principle, conclusion), and they incline to those acts.
claims: A science of many attributes of one subject is one numerically simple habit (reported).
The first generating act produces the whole reality of a habit (reported).
Cognitive habits are increased by acts of different species (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e408.summary: First argument for the second opinion: when conclusions are known from principles, the principles are known more perfectly, and a conclusion known alongside another is known better. This would not hold unless one habit covered them all.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e421.summary: Second argument: according to Posterior Analytics I, of one thing as one there is one science.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e428.summary: Third argument: otherwise metaphysics would be one only by unity of aggregation.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e433.summary: Fourth argument: otherwise there would be no more unity within metaphysics than between mathematics and metaphysics.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e440.summary: Fifth argument: among essentially ordered things one must reach a first, so among sciences there is one first and therefore one in number.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e447.summary: Begins the critique of the second opinion: the 'formal mode of consideration' that supposedly unifies the science must lie either on the side of the intellect or on the side of the object.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e466.summary: Neither works. On the intellect's side, diverse modes of consideration can concern the very same conclusion without yielding distinct sciences, since on the opponent's view one conclusion cannot belong to both mathematics and metaphysics. On the object's side, such rationes cannot be distinguished in the object, since there is no such distinction ex natura rei on their view.
claims: Modes of consideration on the side of the intellect do not individuate sciences.
There is no distinction of such rationes in the object itself.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e484.summary: Argues that principles, conclusions and diverse conclusions have distinct habits. Things of the same kind, equally perfect, in an equally disposed patient, have effects of the same kind. A strong habit generated only from acts about a principle and a no stronger habit from acts about a conclusion do not have the same effects: on the opponents' view and by experience, only the latter inclines to the conclusion. So they are not of the same kind.
claims: Equally perfect causes of the same kind in an equally disposed patient have effects of the same kind.
A habit from acts about a principle does not incline to acts about the conclusion.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e513.summary: Objection: the principle-habit, once perfected, could incline to the conclusion-act, but only when generated or increased by acts about the conclusion.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e522.summary: Reply: for a cause to have its effect it does not matter what produced it, if it is of the same kind and equally perfect. Heat warms equally whether produced by fire, the sun or God alone, especially when it does not depend on its producer for existence. A habit does not depend for its existence on the acts that produced it. So if equally perfect it would have the same effect, but a habit from a thousand acts about a principle cannot do what one from two acts about a conclusion can. So they differ in species.
claims: A cause's effect does not depend on the origin of the cause if it is of the same kind and perfection.
A habit does not depend for its existence on the acts that generated it.
Habits of principle and conclusion differ in species.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e553.summary: Confirmation: when a total efficient cause is applied to a sufficiently disposed patient, action follows. Given a principle-habit, the total cause of the conclusion-act would be present, so the act would follow. Against the reply that different degrees incline to different acts: degrees of the same kind differ only by intensity. A habit from a thousand acts about a principle differs more in intensity from one generated by a single act than do the principle-habit and conclusion-habit, so the latter pair should differ less in effects. If degrees from acts about a principle cannot produce specifically distinct acts, neither can these, which contradicts experience.
claims: A total efficient cause applied to a disposed patient produces its action.
Degrees of the same kind differ only by intensity.
Treating habit differences as differences of degree contradicts experience.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e621.summary: Further confirmation: what is contrary to a weak form is all the more contrary to an intense form of the same kind. If error about a conclusion is contrary to a weak habit of knowing it, it would be more contrary to a very intense principle-habit of the same kind, which is plainly false.
claims: What is contrary to a weak form is more contrary to an intense form of the same kind.
Error about a conclusion is compatible with a strong habit of a principle.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e642.summary: Restates the general argument: if the degrees are of the same kind, the effect will be of the same kind.
claims: Degrees of the same kind have effects of the same kind.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e649.summary: Second argument, following a certain doctor: in geometry, understanding of some principles and knowledge of some conclusions coexist with an erroneous disposition about another conclusion. Opposite habits cannot exist together in one subject concerning the same complex, so the habit of those principles and conclusions is not the habit of the conclusion one errs about.
claims: Knowledge of some principles and conclusions coexists with error about another conclusion.
Opposite habits about the same complex cannot coexist in one subject.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e669.summary: Objection: contraries can coexist when weak, or when one is at the lowest degree and the other at the highest. A habit inclining to understand only one principle is weak and imperfect and so compatible with error about a conclusion, while a perfect habit covering both principle and conclusion is not.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e687.summary: Counter-case: suppose the principle-habit is at its highest, increased by thousands of acts about the principle alone, and the conclusion-habit is generated by a few acts about both principle and conclusion.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e703.summary: Then the first habit is clearly more perfect than the second, yet error about the conclusion is compatible with the first and not the second, so the compatibility is not due to the first habit's imperfection. Another reply is introduced: the argument proves the degrees distinct but not specifically distinct.
claims: Compatibility with error is not due to imperfection of the principle-habit.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e719.summary: Answers that reply: whenever something in a perfect degree coexists with one contrary and another in a perfect degree does not, the two differ in species (sweetness and blackness with respect to whiteness). Things of the same species, both perfect, are compatible and incompatible with the same things. Perfect knowledge of another principle or conclusion coexists with error about a conclusion, while perfect knowledge of that conclusion does not, so these differ in species.
claims: Two perfect forms differing in compatibility with a contrary differ in species.
Perfect knowledge of other truths is compatible with error about a conclusion, and perfect knowledge of that conclusion is not.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e766.summary: Confirmation: things primarily contrary to specifically distinct things are themselves specifically distinct, as heat and moisture are contrary to cold and dryness. Errors about two false universal conclusions differ in species because they are formally incompatible, so the sciences contrary to them, and likewise sciences of distinct conclusions generally, differ in species. Other arguments rely on these two.
claims: What is primarily contrary to specifically distinct things is itself specifically distinct.
Errors about different conclusions differ in species.
Sciences of distinct conclusions differ in species.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e795.summary: Argues that theology is simply not one habit: evident knowledge of something necessary and knowledge of something contingent, whether evident or not, are not numerically one habit. Theology contains evident knowledge of necessary truths (that God exists, is good, one, wise, as in the first question), inevident knowledge of necessary truths (that God is three and one), and knowledge of contingent truths (that God is incarnate, that God beatifies the soul).
claims: Evident knowledge of a necessary truth and knowledge of a contingent truth are not one habit.
Theology includes evident necessary, inevident necessary, and contingent knowledge.
That God exists and is good, one and wise can be evidently known.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e824.summary: Announces the structure of Ockham's answer: first about habits in general, then about theology in particular.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e831.summary: First thesis: a habit acquired only from acts about a principle is distinct from the habit of the conclusion. A cause is always distinct from its effect, whether a per se cause or a sine qua non, and the principle-habit is a cause of the conclusion-habit in one of these ways. Someone with only the principle-habit who then applies another premise will know the conclusion evidently, and not without the principle-habit.
claims: A habit of a principle is distinct from a habit of the conclusion.
Cause and effect are always distinct.
The habit of a principle is in some way a cause of knowing the conclusion.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e860.summary: Further, knowledge of principles is more perfect than knowledge of conclusions (Posterior Analytics I), and nothing is more perfect than itself. Second thesis: distinct conclusions have distinct habits. Universal and particular demonstration differ in species, so either knowledge of premises or of conclusions differs in species. There is no more reason for the premises' habits to differ than the conclusions', so the conclusions' cognitions always differ in species.
claims: Knowledge of principles is more perfect than knowledge of conclusions.
Distinct conclusions have distinct habits.
Universal and particular demonstrations differ in species.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e893.summary: Third thesis: there can be one habit of some principles together with conclusions. Whatever can be the object of one act can be the object of one habit, and premises and conclusion can be grasped in one act, since a syllogism of several propositions can be understood by one act just as a proposition of several terms is.
claims: There can be one habit covering both principles and a conclusion.
Whatever can be the object of one act can be the object of one habit.
A whole syllogism can be understood in a single act.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e916.summary: Generalizes: habits and acts are always proportioned in identity and diversity, since a habit has as much identity or diversity as the acts generating or increasing it. A habit relates to its object neither as object nor as cause except through the act: it inclines to the object only by inclining to the act and is caused by the object only through the act. So identity or diversity of habits must be inferred from that of acts, not directly from objects.
claims: Habits are proportioned to acts in identity and diversity.
A habit relates to its object only through the act.
Identity of habits should be inferred from acts, not objects.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e947.summary: Interprets Aristotle: 'one science' means either a collection of many habits with a determinate order, or many known conclusions so ordered. Conclusions can be ordered by predicates (properties of magnitude, figure and its species shown of figure, which yields particular conclusions), by subjects (properties of animal shown of animal and its inferiors), or by both. Such order makes a science one in a way others lacking it are not, and this is how Aristotle and other doctors speak.
claims: Aristotle's 'one science' is an ordered collection of habits or conclusions.
Conclusions may be ordered by predicates, by subjects, or by both.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e995.summary: Turns to theology. Taken as including infused faith, theology is numerically one, since infused faith is numerically one (to be treated in Book III). Taken as acquired faith plus evident habits of propositions and inferences and apprehensive habits of complexes and incomplexes, it is not one. Acquired faith is not numerically one because acts of belief differ in species, as a heretic has acquired faith about one article and error about another.
claims: Infused faith is numerically one.
Acquired faith is not numerically one, because acts of belief differ in species.
A heretic can have acquired faith about one article and error about another.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e1034.summary: Likewise, apprehensive habits are distinct, because they are separable: one can be strongly inclined to think about one article and not another.
claims: Apprehensive habits are distinct because separable.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e1043.summary: Raises the first of four doubts: how the habits of principle and conclusion compare in perfection.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e1052.summary: Second doubt: whether the habit of principles causes the habit of the conclusion.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e1058.summary: Third doubt: why posit a habit of principles at all, since the intellect is determined to principles, especially self-evident ones, and a determined power needs no determining habit.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e1069.summary: Fourth doubt: what kind of habit is the single habit covering premises and conclusion.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e1076.summary: Answers the first doubt: the habit of principles is more perfect, since a habit's nobility lies in its greater evidence or nobler object. The conclusion has no nobler object, because every partial object of the conclusion is a partial object of some principle, and knowledge of the conclusion is not more evident than that of the premises but the reverse.
claims: The habit of principles is more perfect than the habit of conclusions.
A habit's nobility lies in evidence or in the nobility of its object.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e1096.summary: Answers the second doubt: knowledge of principles is the efficient cause of knowledge of the conclusion, in that it is acquired through it. Objection: the necessary and everlasting has no cause, and the conclusion is necessary.
claims: Knowledge of principles efficiently causes knowledge of conclusions.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e1109.summary: Further objection: every secondary efficient cause can exist without its effect, since God can suspend secondary causality, but it is impossible for the premises to be necessary without the conclusion being necessary.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e1120.summary: Replies: knowledge of the premises causes knowledge of the conclusion, though the premises do not cause the conclusion. The first holds because a cause is that upon whose being something follows and without which it is not posited, and in such an intellect knowledge of the conclusion follows on knowledge of the premises. The second holds because an intellect possessing the terms can form the conclusion whether or not the premises are posited. A conclusion is 'necessary' not because it always actually exists and is true (except perhaps in the divine intellect) but because it is true and can never be false.
claims: Knowledge of premises causes knowledge of the conclusion; the premises do not cause the conclusion.
A cause is that upon whose being the effect follows and without which it does not.
A necessary proposition is one that is true and can never be false, not one that always exists.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e1152.summary: Answers the further objection: Ockham grants that knowledge of the premises can be posited without knowledge of the conclusion, so knowledge of the conclusion is contingent, being a creature, though it concerns a necessary object in the sense explained.
claims: Knowledge of the conclusion is contingent as a created act, though its object is necessary.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e1163.summary: Defers the third doubt, about the need for a habit of principles, to Book III.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e1168.summary: Answers the fourth doubt: the single habit covering premises and conclusion is wisdom (sapientia). It is equivalently understanding and science, since it concerns what they concern, so wisdom concerns many truths, not one. Every necessary proposition is a principle (object of understanding) or a conclusion (object of science), so if wisdom concerned one truth it would not differ from them.
claims: The habit covering both premises and conclusion is wisdom.
Wisdom is equivalently understanding and science.
Wisdom concerns many truths, not a single one.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e1199.summary: Confirms from Nicomachean Ethics VI: the wise person has demonstration about everything, so wisdom is a demonstration or knowledge of demonstration, covering principles and conclusions. Chapter 8 says wisdom is the most certain science and the wise must not only know what follows from principles but speak truly about principles, so wisdom is understanding and science.
claims: Wisdom covers both principles and conclusions (Aristotle).

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e1219.summary: Interprets the authority: wisdom concerns principles and conclusions and is understanding and science, but not really and formally, or it would not be a distinct habit. It is so equivalently, by concerning the same objects.
claims: Wisdom is not really and formally identical with understanding and science.
Wisdom is understanding and science equivalently.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e1235.summary: Objections: then wisdom would concern all necessary truths, and wisdom would be identical with demonstration, which includes both principles and conclusions.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e1245.summary: Answers the first objection: wisdom is taken strictly or broadly. Strictly, it concerns only the noblest things (Ethics VI.8; Metaphysics I). Broadly, it is any habit concerning first principles and the conclusions following from them, and in this sense it is found even in the mechanical arts, as Aristotle calls Phidias a wise stonemason.
claims: Wisdom strictly concerns the noblest things.
Wisdom broadly is any habit of first principles with their conclusions, including in the mechanical arts.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e1274.summary: Answers the second objection: not every demonstration involves wisdom, but every demonstration propter quid involves wisdom broadly taken. In no art is one who knows only the 'that' called wise, but one who knows the 'why'.
claims: Every propter quid demonstration involves wisdom broadly taken.
Knowing only the 'that' does not make one wise.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e1285.summary: Answers the first argument for the second opinion: when conclusions are known from principles, the principles are known more perfectly because an act concerning them is elicited and their habit is intensified. The same holds when one conclusion is known alongside another. But eliciting an act of knowing one conclusion does not make another be known more perfectly.
claims: Principles are known better through use in deriving conclusions, because their habit is intensified by an act.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e1303.summary: Answers the second argument: one subject has one science by unity of order, as an army or city is one, not numerically. Taking 'unity of aggregation' for any unity that is not numerical, such a science is one by aggregation. A science is numerically one only if it concerns one conclusion, or inclines to one act of knowing a conclusion through principles. There are as many sciences as conclusions, even with the same subject and different predicates, since science concerns the predicate as much as the subject, both being parts of the conclusion.
claims: A science of one subject is one by unity of order, not numerically.
A science is numerically one only if it concerns one conclusion.
There are as many sciences as conclusions.
A science concerns the predicate as much as the subject.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e1342.summary: Answers the third argument: metaphysics is indeed one by unity of aggregation.
claims: Metaphysics is one by unity of aggregation.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e1349.summary: Concedes the consequence that we lack many metaphysical and natural sciences: in the present state everyone lacks many partial sciences.
claims: In the present state everyone lacks many partial sciences.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e1357.summary: Answers the fifth argument: one must stop at a first, and that first is the science of one first conclusion, or a single habit inclining to know that first conclusion through prior principles.
claims: The first science is the knowledge of one first conclusion.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e1368.summary: Answers the first principal argument: theology's habit includes many habits, among which one is first, whatever it may be.
claims: The habit of theology includes many habits, one of which is first.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e1375.summary: Answers the second principal argument: one genus of subject has one science if the property is one; otherwise the science is one by unity of order.

wo8uy7-d1e154-d1e1382.summary: Answers the third principal argument: metaphysics, understood as the whole book of the Metaphysics, is one only by such unity of order.
claims: Metaphysics as a whole is one only by unity of order.

wo8uy7-d1e154.summary: Prologue question 8, annexed to the third principal question, asks whether the habit of theology is numerically one. Ockham rejects two opinions that affirm this. Against the first, that theology is one through the formal ratio of 'divinely revealed', he argues that unity of formal object neither entails nor is entailed by unity of power or habit: sense and intellect, intuition and abstraction, intellect and will, science and error share objects, while sight has distinct formal objects. Also, revelability would make geometry theology. Against the second (Scotist-style) opinion, that a science is one simple habit grown by different acts, he argues that principle-habits and conclusion-habits must differ in species: equal causes of the same kind have like effects, and compatibility with error differs among perfect habits. His own theses: habits of principles and conclusions are distinct; distinct conclusions have distinct habits; one habit can cover premises and conclusion when grasped by one act. Habits are always proportioned to acts, not objects. A 'science' in Aristotle's sense is one only by unity of order or aggregation, and there are as many sciences as conclusions. Theology as infused faith is one, but as acquired faith plus evident and apprehensive habits it is many, since it includes evident necessary, inevident necessary and contingent truths. Answering doubts, he holds that the principle-habit is more perfect, that knowledge of premises causes knowledge of conclusions (though premises do not cause conclusions), and that the habit uniting premises and conclusions is wisdom, which is equivalently understanding and science.
claims: The habit of theology, apart from infused faith, is not numerically one.
Unity or diversity of habits follows unity or diversity of acts, not formal objects.
Habits of distinct conclusions, and of principles and conclusions, differ in species.
Sciences are unified only by unity of order or aggregation.
Knowledge of premises causes knowledge of conclusions.
Wisdom is a habit covering principles and conclusions, equivalently understanding and science.
